'''James J. Gillogly''' (born 5 March 1946) is an American [[computer scientist]] and [[cryptographer]].

==Biography==
===Early life===
His interest in cryptography stems from his boyhood, as did his interest in mathematics.<ref name=lat-UMGTN-CMGVP-TLGE-RVGB>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-11-05-me-65166-story.html|title=UMGTN CMGVP TLGE RVGB : (The Solution to This Headline Is at Bottom of Story)|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|last=Pool|first=Bob|date=5 November 1995|access-date=11 March 2018}}</ref> By junior high he was inventing his own ciphers and challenging his father, entomologist Lorin Gillogly, to solve them.<ref name=lat-UMGTN-CMGVP-TLGE-RVGB/>

Gillogly wrote a chess-playing program in the [[Fortran]] programming language in 1970, and in 1977 he ported the code for "[[Colossal Cave Adventure|Colossal Cave]]" from Fortran to [[C (programming language)|C]].

===Education===
He graduated from [[Carnegie Mellon University]] in 1978, receiving a [[Ph.D.]] in computer science. He was advised by [[Allen Newell]], with his dissertation titled "Performance Analysis of the Technology Chess Program".<ref name=math-genealogy-proj>{{cite news|url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=50361|title=James Gillogly|work=[[The Mathematics Genealogy Project]]}}</ref>

===Career===
Gillogly worked as a computer scientist at [[RAND]], specializing in system design and development, and [[computer security]]. He has written several articles about technology and cryptography, is currently the editor of the "Cipher Exchange" column for ''[[American Cryptogram Association|The Cryptogram]]'', and was president of the [[American Cryptogram Association]].

Gillogly was one of the earliest authors of personal computer software, writing utility programs,<ref>{{cite web|title=BUSS Newsletter #21, January 1980|url=http://toolworks.com/history/BUSS%2021%20First%20Software%20Published%202-80.pdf|page=2}}</ref> games and a computerized cookbook published by the [[Software Toolworks]] beginning in 1980.

===Cryptanalysis===
He is best known for his work solving or debunking some of the world's most famous unsolved codes. In 1980 he wrote a paper on unusual strings in the [[Beale ciphers]], and he received international media attention for being the first person to publicly solve parts 1-3 on the [[CIA]]'s [[Kryptos]] sculpture in 1999. He also coordinates a large mailing list about the ciphers in the [[Voynich Manuscript]].  On the [[Public Broadcasting Service|PBS]] website, they report that he has been called "arguably the best non-government cryptanalyst in the U.S." in the field of classical (historical) cryptosystems.<ref>[https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/decoding/]</ref>

In 1995 he deciphered a text enciphered by [[Robert H. Thouless]] who had hoped the message could prove that the dead could communicate with the living.<ref name=lat-UMGTN-CMGVP-TLGE-RVGB/> Gillogly wrote his own software to decipher the text, which was in a variant of the [[playfair cipher]].<ref name=lat-UMGTN-CMGVP-TLGE-RVGB/>
